articles.summary: PTFI Supports Major Mangrove Restoration Effort in Indonesia mboyle Wed, 08/19/2026 - 08:37 Post Image August 19, 2026 - PT Freeport Indonesia leaders worked alongside government officials and community members in West Nusa Tenggara (NTB), Indonesia, to support a large-scale mangrove restoration project that strengthens coastal ecosystems and local livelihoods. Mangroves are salt-tolerant trees and shrubs that grow along tropical coastlines, especially in areas where freshwater and seawater mix. PTFI President Director Tony Wenas recently joined Minister of Environment and Head of the Environmental Management Agency Mohammad Jumhur Hidayat, NTB Governor Lalu Muhammad Iqbal and local residents for a mangrove planting event in Labuan Alas Village, Sumbawa Regency. Jumhur praised PTFI's commitment to supporting Indonesia's national mangrove planting program, which aligns with the Ministry of Environment's initiative to plant 2 billion trees in response to global environmental challenges. Growing effort PTFI has rehabilitated nearly 500 hectares of mangroves in NTB and is targeting the rehabilitation of 12,000 hectares across Indonesia, particularly in Papua. (One hectare is the equivalent of about 2.5 acres.) "Mangroves play a vital role in protecting coastal ecosystems, absorbing carbon and supporting community livelihoods," Jumhur said. PTFI's mangrove restoration program in NTB covers 484 hectares, Wenas said. The company plans to plant 1.5 million mangrove seedlings across the region by the end of 2026. "In addition to supporting the successful rehabilitation of coastal areas, this involvement serves as a means of raising public awareness and concern for mangrove conservation and the importance of sustainably protecting the environment," Wenas said. The effort stems from a 2023 cooperation agreement between PTFI, the Peat and Mangrove Restoration Agency and Indonesia's environmental authorities. The program supports national mangrove restoration goals outside PTFI's operational area in Papua. PTFI's mangrove restoration work also extends to Papua, where the company has planted about 5.5 million mangrove seedlings across more than 2,184 hectares in Mimika Regency. Widespread participation The NTB project has created opportunities for local communities. About 1,500 residents have participated in activities ranging from seedling cultivation to planting and maintenance. Muhammad Tisnaini of the Sumbawa Mangrove Community said the program has helped coastal residents build expertise in mangrove conservation while improving local fisheries. "We have mentored five community groups who are now able to produce seedlings and plant them independently," Tisnaini said. "The presence of mangroves also helps fishermen because they provide habitat for various types of fish." The planting activity highlights ongoing collaboration among government, business, academic and community partners to protect coastal ecosystems, support biodiversity and strengthen natural defenses against climate change. Photo: PTFI President Director Tony Wenas (right) and Minister of Environment and Head of the Environmental Management Agency Mohammad Jumhur Hidayat show the mangrove seedlings being planted.
articles.title: PTFI Supports Major Mangrove Restoration Effort in Indonesia

articles.summary: El Abra Commemorates 30 Years of Operation mboyle Thu, 08/27/2026 - 09:28 Post Image August 27, 2026 - Freeport’s El Abra operation in Chile is commemorating 30 years of mining, which began with the production of its first copper cathode August 10, 1996. A landing page that traces the site’s key milestones since it opened has been added to El Abra’s website. In addition, a book that profiles 30 El Abra workers and the contributions they make both on and off the job is being distributed to all employees. “These 30 years represent much more than an operational journey,” said Boris Medina, President-El Abra. “They reflect three decades of relationships built with employees, contractors, communities and local organizations. We are proud of what we have achieved together and confident that El Abra’s future will continue to be shaped alongside the people and communities that have accompanied us throughout this journey.” The anniversary comes at a pivotal time for the mine. El Abra currently is advancing through the environmental permitting process for its Operational Continuity Project. The initiative is designed to extend the mine’s life for several more decades and enable a future expansion that would triple current copper production through the addition of a new concentrator plant and the use of desalinated seawater. Beyond its mining activities, El Abra has built long-term relationships with neighboring communities, supporting programs focused on education, local economic development, cultural heritage and environmental stewardship. Photo: Diego Moya Palta, Maintenance Engineer II, is one of 30 El Abra employees profiled in a book that helps commemorate 30 years of operations.
articles.title: El Abra Commemorates 30 Years of Operation

articles.summary: Cerro Verde Copper Coin Honors U.S.-Peru Relations mboyle Sat, 08/08/2026 - 12:10 Post Image August 8, 2026 - A commemorative coin crafted from copper produced at Cerro Verde was unveiled during a recent ceremony at Miami Dade College in Florida, celebrating the bicentennial of diplomatic relations between the United States and Peru. U.S. Ambassador to Peru Bernie Navarro unveiled the copper replica of the official commemorative coin issued by the Central Reserve Bank of Peru. Julia Torreblanca, Senior Vice President of Corporate Affairs-Cerro Verde, was among a group of dignitaries who spoke at the event. Created specifically for the bicentennial celebration, the unique piece was made from 136 pounds of high-purity copper (99.999 percent) produced at Cerro Verde's electrowinning plant in Arequipa. Measuring 35 inches in diameter and almost half an inch thick, the replica of the official coin features two iconic landmarks: Miami, Florida’s Freedom Tower and Peru's Machu Picchu. Peruvian artist Gino Torres transformed the Arequipa copper into a work of historical importance. "Freeport's significant presence in Arequipa reflects a long-term, responsible U.S. investment, thousands of Peruvian jobs and decades of collaboration,” Torreblanca said to those in attendance at the ceremony. “When we were asked to help commemorate 200 years of diplomatic relations between the United States and Peru, we did not hesitate. “This copper comes from Peruvian soil, was produced by proud and responsible miners in Arequipa, shaped by a Peruvian artist and now honors a bond between two nations that continues to grow stronger." Torreblanca also thanked the more than 5,400 Cerro Verde employees and contract workers whose efforts helped make the project possible. She also noted that, in addition to supplying copper and molybdenum, Cerro Verde supports water infrastructure and community development in Arequipa and across Peru.
articles.title: Cerro Verde Copper Coin Honors U.S.-Peru Relations

articles.summary: Freeport Celebrates Future Talent at 2026 University Intern Conference mboyle Tue, 08/25/2026 - 09:17 Post Image August 25, 2026 - Freeport’s future was on full display as the company’s 2026 University Intern Conference brought its summer class to corporate headquarters in Phoenix for two days of presentations, networking and celebration. This year, 193 interns joined Freeport from 67 universities across the country. They gained hands-on experience in disciplines such as engineering, metallurgy, chemistry, geology, business administration, communications and health and safety. Of that group, 117 were selected to present their summer projects to fellow interns, mentors and company leaders. Comprehensive program Held July 29-30 in Phoenix, the conference paired those project presentations with speakers and breakout sessions spanning the many technical fields that power modern mining. Day 1 featured a keynote from Stacey Koon, Vice President-Health, Safety and Technical Training. Koon traced her own winding career, from corporate human resources to an expatriate assignment in Chile, to serving as a General Manager in Morenci, to leading health and safety, and encouraged interns to embrace the unknown. “I learned to be comfortable being uncomfortable,” Koon said. “When you’re uncomfortable, that’s when you’re learning.” President and Chief Executive Officer Kathleen Quirk also made an impromptu appearance the first day. After the conference broke into breakout sessions, she quietly slipped into several of the rooms, listened as interns presented their summer projects and offered comments and questions to the presenters. “One of the things that’s so important about you coming into the company is that you’re bringing new perspectives, new ideas and new ways to do things,” she told the interns. “We want to listen to people who aren’t afraid to ask the hard questions.” Samahara Quintana Chavez, who expects to graduate from the University of Texas at El Paso this December, spent this summer as an intern in Operational Excellence and was one of the presenters at the event. “The conference helped me realize that my contributions can extend beyond my immediate team,” she said. “Seeing others engage with my project and hearing how it could be valuable in different areas of the company gave me a better understanding of the broader impact our work can have. It reinforced my interest in pursuing a career where I can continue driving improvements, collaborating across teams and creating solutions that help others.” Freeport’s future workforce For Freeport’s Talent Acquisition team, the conference caps a program that has become one of the company’s most important talent pipelines. “Freeport’s internship program is more than a summer experience; it’s an investment in our future workforce,” said Alyssa Kohn, Talent Acquisition Supervisor. “As Freeport continues to grow, the program serves as an important talent pipeline, helping us develop future professionals who may return as full-time employees and contribute to the company’s long-term success.” That pipeline is a proven one. Over the past five years, an average of 83 percent of Freeport interns have received some form of offer, whether a return internship or a new-graduate role, Kohn said. Photos (top to bottom): Samahara Quintana Chavez, Operational Excellence Intern, presents at the 2026 University Summer Intern Conference; Alexander Fosu (left) and Oscar Zapana Gago, Chino’s Project Engineering interns, collaborated on the winning entry in the intern photo contest; Aadish Velmani, Geology Intern-Technology Center Tucson (left); Renzo Omar Solis Vega, Hydrometallurgy Research and Development Intern-Morenci; Zohreh Kazemi Motlagh, Geology Intern-Chino; and Mariam Koanda, Mine Engineer I-Chino, who was one of this year’s intern mentors.
articles.title: Freeport Celebrates Future Talent at 2026 University Intern Conference

articles.summary: Miguel Palacios Bids Farewell to Company mboyle Tue, 08/04/2026 - 11:56 Post Image August 4, 2026 - Miguel Palacios recalled a breakroom conversation with Kathleen Quirk that captured his approach to work during more than four decades with the company. Palacios was in the midst of his tenure as Vice President-North America Smelting and Refining with responsibility for the company’s Miami and El Paso operations several years back when he encountered Quirk, now the company’s President and Chief Executive Officer. “One day, Kathleen asked me what I was doing in Miami because things were running so well," Palacios said of the conversation that took place at the company’s Hub in Phoenix. "My response was that any good results in Miami were due to a great team there, competent and highly motivated.” It’s his former colleagues, the people with whom he shared every professional success and challenge, that Palacios speaks about first when recalling the highlights of his years spent with Atlantic Copper and Freeport. Palacios retired this summer following a career that took him from a young metallurgist in Spain to leadership roles across Freeport's global smelting and refining operations. Reflecting on Retirement "It feels a little bit strange," Palacios said just days after retirement. "It's a contradictory feeling. After 44 years in business and 42 with the company, it's difficult to imagine not being part of it every day." Palacios joined Atlantic Copper in 1984 as a process engineer and metallurgist. Within a few years, he was promoted to smelter superintendent, beginning a steady progression through increasingly senior leadership roles. He later served as Technology Director before becoming Senior Vice President of Atlantic Copper's operation in Huelva, Spain. His career expanded beyond Spain in 2019 when he accepted an assignment to lead Freeport's Miami smelter and El Paso refinery operations through a period of transition. "They asked if I needed a few days to think about it," Palacios recalled. "I said no. If the company believes I can provide the best service there, I'm ready." With that, Palacios and his wife, Esperanza Morillo León, who worked in Atlantic Copper’s communications department and later accepted a role in Freeport’s communications department in Phoenix, were off to Arizona. During his tenure in the U.S., the smelter operations underwent significant improvements, including modernization and initiatives focused on reliability, workplace conditions and employee engagement. Besides improving technical aspects and identifying critical investments for Miami and El Paso, Palacios also addressed what some might call the softer parts of the business: tidiness and cleanliness, maintenance, new paint and comfortable common work areas. Working in a pleasant environment, Palacios believed, carries a significant motivating effect and fosters a sense of pride in belonging. "When people feel proud of where they work, things begin to change," he said. "Before we had time to invest in major projects, production and availability were already improving." Return to Spain With the Miami and El Paso operations back on solid footing, Palacios and Morillo León headed back to Atlantic Copper in 2022, Palacios as Senior Vice President of Business Development and Morillo León as Director of Communications. Once back in Spain, Palacios also played a key role in the Manyar Project, PT Freeport Indonesia’s new smelter and refinery complex. His involvement spanned the full project lifecycle, from process selection and site evaluation through basic design and detailed engineering. During commissioning in 2024 and 2025, he devoted most of his time to the project, while also leading Atlantic Copper’s senior technical team. With his work at the new smelter winding down, Palacios was able to follow Morillo León, who had retired in 2024, into the next chapter of their lives. For both, retirement may mean not reporting to work each day, but it doesn’t mean resting idle either. Morillo León is active in local theater, while Palacios plans to immerse himself in his longtime hobbies of reading and photography while taking on a long-postponed goal of completing his doctorate from the University of Seville, where he earned his master’s degree in chemical engineering in 1982. As he turns the page on his Freeport career, Palacios is heartened by the calls and emails he has received from a countless number of colleagues whom he has mentored and learned from. His outgoing message to the next generation of employees isn’t as much about hard skills and business acumen; it is taking a sincere interest in those around you, showing you care about their success as much as you do your own. "I've known many brilliant people who never reached their full potential because they didn't understand the role of people," he said. "My advice is simple: stay focused on people, your bosses, your peers, the people who work for you. In my case, that was the key to everything I accomplished." Photo: Miguel Palacios and his wife, Esperanza Morillo León, spend much of their time in Huelva, Spain, on the coast of the Atlantic Ocean.
articles.title: Miguel Palacios Bids Farewell to Company
